title: Classes, interfaces and state
goal: Design operations that prevent callers from violating related constraints.

prerequisites.text: Modules 1–4: input, functions, sequences, ownership, testing and multifile builds.

sections.title: An interface is a set of promises
paragraphs: Stock models a quantity between zero and one hundred. receive and ship are not merely ways to assign a field: they define valid transitions. Receiving cannot exceed capacity, and shipping cannot create a negative quantity. Before coding, describe the pre-call state, success condition, resulting state and behaviour on rejection.

Test the public interface as a client who cannot access a private field. A quantity() observer can establish a successful delivery and preservation after rejection. A test that bypasses access control becomes tied to implementation. It would obstruct a representation change even if the application's observable result remained unchanged.

sections.title: Private and public
paragraphs: class and struct differ in default access: private for class, public for struct. Their underlying mechanisms are the same. Private access restricts ordinary use at compile time; it neither encrypts memory nor creates a security boundary. The laboratory hides the field and exposes operations. This is a code organization rule rather than secret protection.

An interface declaration should provide the types, parameters and results a client needs. Do not return a mutable reference to the internal quantity: a caller could assign minus one and bypass validation. In larger types a pointer or view also needs a lifetime contract. For now the observer returns a small int by value.

sections.title: Worked model
paragraphs: Design operations that prevent callers from violating related constraints.
steps: The const view calls quantity only: output 0 8.

sections.title: Const and observation
paragraphs: A quantity() const method can be called through const Stock&. Inside it, this points to a const object, so ordinary field assignment is forbidden. The method marks an observation and helps the compiler catch accidental changes. receive and ship are not const because a successful call changes domain state.

Const does not automatically imply thread safety or the absence of external effects. A method could write to cout, and mutable fields follow special rules. Our observer deliberately performs no input or output. That is a stronger design agreement than the keyword alone. A free printing function can use a const reference without owning the object.

sections.title: Related fields and domain atomicity
paragraphs: Window has two fields with the invariant low_≤high_. Two independent setters could create an invalid intermediate state when changing [0,0] to [2,7]. reset(a,b) accepts both values, checks their relationship and only then assigns them. This atomicity concerns domain meaning; it does not describe synchronization between threads.

After reset(2,7), the worked example calls reset(9,1) and receives false. contains(4) remains true, while contains(8) is false. This checks preservation as well as rejection. Validation before small nonthrowing assignments suffices here. Operations that allocate memory need a separate exception guarantee analysis later in the module.

sections.title: Choosing an error result
paragraphs: A bool works when a caller only needs to know whether an operation succeeded. If callers must distinguish insufficient stock from a negative argument, introduce a result enum or a structure with an error code. Do not encode failure as a valid quantity: zero can be a normal stock level. Exceptions follow resource management later in this module.

An operation rejection and an input syntax error belong to different layers. A negative amount is a correctly parsed int but is rejected by Stock. A letter in place of an amount fails parsing and produces invalid. Classify the error before deciding which layer has enough information to handle it. This improves messages and test stability.

sections.title: Contract boundary check
paragraphs: Design operations that prevent callers from violating related constraints.
steps: reset(9,1) rejects before either field is assigned.
Four is inside and eight outside: output 0 1 0.

sections.title: Executing commands step by step
paragraphs: Input contains n pairs: a plus or minus sign and an integer amount. After validating all pairs, the application creates Stock and executes commands in order. Receiving eight, shipping nine and shipping three produces states zero, eight, eight, five, with one rejection. Reordering commands can change the result; these are events, not an unordered collection of numbers.

receive checks n<0 before comparing n to the remaining capacity. ship checks n<0 and n>quantity_. No rejected path writes the field. Locate that property in the program and create a separate test for each condition. A maximum-int case demonstrates one safe rejection rather than promising arbitrary-precision arithmetic.

sections.title: A negative compilation check
paragraphs: A small diagnostic example tries to read s.quantity_ from main. Compilation must fail because that member is private. This is an expected compile error, not an executable demonstration or a runtime failure. Compare it with s.quantity(), which uses the public contract and leaves state unchanged.

Keep these checks separate from the working application. Do not add a second main to the same executable or leave the intentional error in its primary file. Diagnostic wording varies between compilers; the access restriction is what matters. Memory inspection or reinterpret_cast would not test the interface and is not an appropriate workaround.

sections.title: Reviewing an interface
paragraphs: Present a transition table and explain why every public method preserves the invariant. Add a requirement that partial shipping is either forbidden or explicitly supported. Show the changed contract and tests before editing implementation. Preserving an interface does not mean preserving every accidental behaviour that an earlier implementation happened to expose.

Also check const usage and the absence of a mutable alias to the field. A good interface makes invalid actions difficult and valid actions understandable. The next lesson answers the remaining lifecycle questions: how an object obtains its initial state, which parts are created first and when automatic cleanup occurs.

options: Quantity is preserved and the caller receives false.
Quantity is always reset to zero.
selfcheck.feedback: ship checks its argument and available quantity before assignment. On rejection the caller therefore sees the previous quantity and false, rather than zeroing or a negative quantity.

selfcheck.prompt: Why not return int& to the quantity?
options: A reference must copy the field.
A caller could bypass the checked operations.
An int cannot be returned by value.
selfcheck.feedback: A returned int& would let a caller assign -1 without calling ship or receive. Returning a value keeps mutations under class control; a reference is not itself a copy of the field.

options: Yes; it forbids every external effect.
No; const does not synchronize access.
selfcheck.feedback: const restricts ordinary member modification through this object, but supplies no lock and does not exclude external effects. Concurrent access needs a separately chosen synchronization protocol.

selfcheck.prompt: How does amount -1 differ from x?
options: The former parses and is rejected by the domain; the latter fails parsing.
selfcheck.feedback: Minus one parses as an int and then violates the Stock domain constraint. The token x cannot be read as an amount, so input syntax is rejected before commands execute.

selfcheck.prompt: Why does reset take both bounds?
options: To validate their relationship before changing state.
selfcheck.feedback: The invariant relates low and high, so validate the pair before assigning either field. Independent setters can finish a public call with low>high even when the caller intended a valid final interval.

selfcheck.prompt: Replace two interval setters with one operation.

practice.title: Laboratory: Classes, interfaces and state
practice.task: Read n=0…20 and n sign/integer pairs. Only + and - are valid. Stock starts at zero and stays in 0…100. + receives and - ships; negative amounts or a violated bound reject without mutation. Print quantity and rejection count. Invalid parsing, sign or extra tokens: invalid.
criteria: Each has success, rejection and resulting state.
It observes a live object and cannot call a mutator.
Quantity remains eight and the result is false.
No completed public operation exposes low>high.
Include source, actual results, an independent case and limits of the conclusion.
practice.hint: A quantity() const method can be called through const Stock&. Inside it, this points to a const object, so ordinary field assignment is forbidden. The method marks an observation and helps the compiler catch accidental changes. receive and ship are not const because a successful call changes domain state.

steps.action: Restate the contract and distinguish malformed input from domain rejection.
Write transition tables for receive and ship.
Explain const Stock& in the example.
Open Task and Code Studio: the task stays alongside the editor on desktop or in a phone tab. Save your own code before replacing an example.
Complete the starter; pending marks unfinished work rather than a correct result.
Run every reference case and record actual stdout and exit status.
Design a result with rejection reasons.
Save source, a verification table and an invariant explanation; add one independent case.

terms.definition: Controlling state through an interface that preserves domain meaning.
Members available to ordinary client code.
Language-restricted access without a promise of encrypted storage.
A method that disallows ordinary mutation of the object through this.
An operation that reports state according to a contract.
A condition required before a valid call.
A promise about result and state when a call finishes.
Completing a related update while preserving a joint invariant.
